tldr: This study reformulates Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) as a Hierarchical MDP, performing closed-loop reinforcement learning over a macro action space of topological graph frontiers to overcome reward sparsity and achieve state-of-the-art results.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed method. A high-level planner (macro MDP) selects frontiers on a topological graph while a training-free heuristic controller (micro MDP) executes movements, dramatically compressing the decision horizon for reinforcement learning.
overview:
In Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE), an agent must follow natural language instructions through unseen continuous environments by executing hundreds of fine-grained low-level control steps (such as forward movements and turns) while interacting with the physical space. In this setting, imitation learning (IL) inevitably suffers from compounding errors caused by distribution shift between training and test states, often causing the agent to deviate from paths and fail. Techniques designed to mitigate this, such as DAgger, hit a ceiling because once an agent deviates from the demonstration path, what constitutes an "expert action" becomes fundamentally ambiguous.

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural solution by learning directly from task outcomes through trial and error. However, running RL directly on micro action spaces spanning hundreds of steps suffers from severe sample inefficiency under sparse completion rewards. Existing studies have compromised by restricting optimization to single-turn language outputs on offline trajectories or introducing dense, greedy distance-to-goal rewards. Unfortunately, these compromises degrade autonomous exploration and cause agents to ignore language instructions.

To address this dilemma, the authors revisited structural abstraction via topological graphs. They reformulated VLN-CE as a Hierarchical Markov Decision Process (Hierarchical MDP), explicitly decoupling high-level planning from low-level control. The high-level planner selects unvisited frontier nodes on the graph as macro actions, leaving low-level movement execution to a training-free heuristic controller. This compresses the decision horizon from hundreds of steps down to just 5 to 20 steps, making closed-loop reinforcement learning (PPO) tractable with practical sample efficiency under sparse outcome rewards. They also introduce an "Action-Aware Value Head" designed to handle the dynamically changing frontier action space. Evaluated on standard R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks, the proposed method substantially outperforms conventional imitation learning models and micro-action RL baselines, setting new state-of-the-art performance.
contributions: Formulated VLN-CE as a topological-graph-based Hierarchical MDP, treating low-level control as state transitions to apply closed-loop reinforcement learning over a high-level macro action space.
Designed an Action-Aware Value Head and a graph-based PPO that incorporate dynamic frontier candidate nodes into the state representation to accurately assess state values.
Demonstrated that reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RFT) after imitation learning (DAgger) yields performance gains that are orthogonal (additive) to dataset scaling.
Achieved state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks, outperforming existing graph-based methods and Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) approaches.

sections.heading: Why topological graphs now? Moving from micro actions to macro decisions
sections.summary: In continuous language navigation (VLN-CE), repeating fine-grained low-level controls leads to compounding errors, exposing the limits of imitation learning. This paper abstracts the environment into a topological graph to substantially compress the decision horizon and efficiently apply closed-loop RL on a macro action space.
sections.details:
Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires a robot in an unseen 3D environment to execute hundreds of low-level control commands (such as moving forward or turning) following natural language instructions to reach a goal. Across this long decision-making process, compounding errors stemming from distribution shifts between training and test states remain a major obstacle.

To tackle this, prior work has relied on abstracting environments into nodes via topological graphs or leveraging the commonsense priors of pre-trained Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). However, imitation learning (behavior cloning and DAgger) relies on the premise that an optimal expert action exists for every state. Once an agent strays off the intended route, defining what the correct expert action should be becomes inherently ambiguous.

The natural path to resolve this is reinforcement learning (RL), which learns from trial and error via environmental feedback. Yet, applying RL directly over a micro action space segmented into granular actions yields an excessively long decision horizon where rewards fail to propagate, resulting in terrible sample efficiency. Prior studies compromised by either settling for open-loop output optimization on offline datasets or designing dense reward functions that encourage geometric distance reduction. Both workarounds, however, hinder autonomous exploration and incentivize agents to bypass language instructions.

The authors addressed this by revisiting structural abstraction with topological graphs. By reformulating VLN-CE as a Hierarchical Markov Decision Process (Hierarchical MDP), they tasked the high-level planner with selecting unvisited candidate locations (frontiers) as "macro actions," while delegating low-level locomotion to existing heuristics. This compresses the decision horizon that RL must solve from hundreds of steps down to just 5 to 20 steps, unlocking efficient closed-loop RL.

sections.heading: The evolution of VLN-CE and past compromises in applying RL
sections.summary: As VLN evolved from discrete to continuous environments, waypoint prediction and topological graphs helped abstract decision-making. Meanwhile, recent LVLM and RL applications have relied on restrictive compromises like open-loop tuning and dense reward shaping; this work realizes genuine closed-loop RL via macro action spaces.
sections.details:
### II-A VLN in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE)
Early VLN-CE research attempted to predict low-level motor commands directly from visual observations and text instructions, but performance plateaued due to the overly fine-grained action space. The turning point was the introduction of waypoint prediction. This abstracted the problem from low-level control to high-level waypoint selection, eventually evolving into methods that organize waypoints into topological graphs and employ Transformers for global path planning. Recently, research using Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) as navigation agents has surged. However, LVLMs struggle with panoramic inputs and tend to rely on monocular fields of view, while also lacking the architectural ability to handle topological spatial structures, forcing them to rely on flat histories of past observations.

### II-B Reinforcement learning (RL) in VLN-CE
While RL has been widely adopted in discrete VLN environments, applying it directly to continuous settings (VLN-CE) has remained exceptionally difficult due to step-count explosion. Reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RFT) following supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has attracted attention in the context of LVLMs, but its applications to VLN-CE have been confined to single-turn language generation on offline trajectory data—effectively an "open-loop" optimization without environment interaction. Furthermore, recent attempts at closed-loop RL relied on dense rewards based on geometric distance to the goal to compensate for the hundreds-of-steps horizon. Consequently, agents learned to take straight-line shortcuts and ignore the instruction text altogether. This paper sets itself apart by adopting a topological macro action space, achieving genuine closed-loop RFT without relying on dense reward shaping.

sections.heading: Graph-based PPO powered by a Hierarchical MDP and an Action-Aware Critic
sections.summary: VLN-CE is cleanly separated into a high-level planner (macro MDP) and a low-level controller (micro MDP). An Action-Aware Value Head is proposed to help the Critic capture dynamic frontier spaces, enabling closed-loop PPO using only sparse rewards that evaluate final trajectory quality.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation: A Hierarchical MDP Perspective
A robot receives panoramic RGB-D observations $O_t$ and outputs discrete motor commands $u_t$ (forward, turn, stop). Treating this as a single MDP causes RL training to collapse over horizons spanning hundreds of steps. This paper instead formalizes the problem as a Hierarchical MDP:
- **Macro MDP (High-level Planner)**: State $s^H_t=(I, \mathcal{H}_t)$ consists of language instruction $I$ and past graph trajectory $\mathcal{H}_t$. Action $a^H_t$ is a macro action chosen from dynamically generated unvisited frontiers (and a stop action). Only at episode termination does it receive an outcome reward $r(s^H_T)$ evaluating alignment with the instruction.
- **Micro MDP (Low-level Controller)**: Executes short-range navigation toward the chosen frontier node. Instead of training this with RL, the authors delegate it to a deterministic heuristic controller (turn, then move forward). The entire micro MDP is thus treated as the environment's state transition function $\mathcal{T}^H$ in the macro MDP.

### III-B Closed-loop RFT via Graph-based PPO
For training the high-level planner, PPO was selected for its on-policy nature and fine-grained per-step credit assignment, avoiding GRPO (which relies on single scalar trajectory evaluations) and off-policy methods like SAC (which suffer from multimodal representation drift on stale replay data).

### III-B 1 Action-Aware Value Estimation
The biggest hurdle in RL over topological graphs is that the available action set (frontiers $\mathcal{A}^H_t$) changes dynamically at each step. If the current node is a dead end and all subsequent frontier options are invalid, the action-value $Q$ drops sharply. A conventional Critic predicting state value $V(s^H_t)$ solely from exploration history $\mathcal{H}_t$ suffers from partial observability because it cannot see forward-looking candidate actions, leading to inaccurate value estimates. To solve this, the authors introduce the Action-Aware Value Head, defining the state via the full topological graph $\mathcal{G}_t$, which encompasses both past history and currently selectable frontiers. This enables the Actor and Critic to share the same multimodal feature backbone, delivering accurate value estimation without extra computational overhead.

### III-B 2 Outcome-Driven Reward and GAE
The reward function eschews dense geometric distance metrics in favor of a sparse outcome reward $R_T$ evaluating final trajectory quality. It combines goal reaching (Success), Path Length weighted by Success (SPL), and normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW) against the reference path. In particular, nDTW measures instruction adherence even on failed episodes, providing strong guidance during early exploration. Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) is computed from this reward to update the policy with PPO.

### III-C Hierarchical Policy Architecture & III-D Training Paradigm
The model processes language with RoBERTa and visual inputs with CLIP alongside a DD-PPO-trained ResNet, fusing multimodal features via Graph-Aware Self-Attention (GASA) enriched with spatial distance and orientation biases. Training follows a three-stage curriculum: pre-training, imitation learning via DAgger (with simultaneous Value Head warm-up), and closed-loop RFT via PPO regularized with KL divergence against the reference policy, converging in roughly 16 hours of RL training.

captions.F2: System architecture of the proposed method. The high-level macro MDP receives language instructions and the topological graph, simultaneously performing frontier selection (Actor) and Action-Aware state value estimation (Critic) from a shared backbone. The low-level micro MDP acts as a deterministic controller, managing state transitions.

sections.heading: Substantial accuracy gains, new SOTA, and the clear edge of macro actions
sections.summary: Evaluated on R2R-CE and RxR-CE in the Habitat simulator, the proposed method achieved new SOTA results. Rigorous comparisons against micro-action RL baselines and alternative RL algorithms highlight the necessity of macro actions and the Action-Aware Value Head.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Comparative Results and SOTA Performance
Experiments were conducted in the Habitat simulator across unseen validation environments (Val-Unseen) on standard benchmarks: R2R-CE (shortest-path instructions) and RxR-CE (long, non-shortest-path instructions). The proposed model already outperformed existing graph-based methods (such as HNR) and 7B-parameter LVLM approaches (like StreamVLN) at the DAgger imitation learning stage, and closed-loop RFT delivered further gains:
- **R2R-CE**: Success Rate (SR) increased from 65.1% to 68.1% (+3.0 points), and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) rose from 53.5% to 57.3% (+3.8 points).
- **RxR-CE**: On this complex multilingual, long-instruction benchmark, it achieved an SR of 62.3% and an nDTW of 66.8%, setting state-of-the-art performance across both datasets.

### IV-C Ablation Studies on the RL Framework
The contribution of each component was verified on R2R-CE:
- **Effectiveness of Action-Aware Value Head**: Replacing it with a conventional history-only Critic caused the SR gain to drop from +3.0 to +1.1 points, while training time increased from 16 to 25 hours because the shared backbone could no longer be used. Exposing dynamic frontier candidates to the Critic is vital.
- **RL Algorithm Comparison**: Compared to PPO (+3.0 SR), GRPO achieved only +1.7 points due to its inability to perform step-level credit assignment. Off-policy SAC gained +2.1 points, but stale representations in the replay buffer disturbed multimodal alignment, and target network updates increased training runtime.
- **Reward Design and Epochs**: Dense geodesic distance-reduction rewards degraded performance by encouraging the agent to take geometric shortcuts while ignoring text instructions. In addition, multi-epoch updates on the same batch caused representation overfitting; strict on-policy training (1-epoch update) proved optimal.

### IV-D Head-to-Head Against Micro Action Spaces
A baseline operating directly on micro motor actions using the same backbone was evaluated. Open-loop RFT on offline trajectories overfitted without improving validation metrics. In-environment closed-loop PPO took 120 hours of training and gained only +0.6 SR, as the horizon was too long for terminal reward credit assignment. Horizon compression via macro actions is indeed the decisive factor for successful closed-loop RL.

### IV-E & IV-F Orthogonality and Qualitative Analysis
Across experiments varying pre-training data from 25% to 100%, the performance boost from RFT (gain in SR + SPL) remained consistently between +6.2 and +7.0 points. This confirms that RFT gains are orthogonal (independent) to dataset scale, addressing fundamental imitation learning bottlenecks. In qualitative examples (Figure F5), when an agent took an incorrect turn early on, the DAgger baseline became confused and failed, whereas the RFT model leveraged topological memory to select an earlier frontier node and execute an effective backtrack to reach the goal.

captions.F5: Comparison of behavior between DAgger and RFT models. At step 5, after an initial incorrect orientation choice, DAgger's action probabilities disperse, leading to confusion and failure. In contrast, the RFT model detects misalignment with the instruction, selects a frontier at the origin, successfully backtracks, and reaches the goal.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: Next challenges for physical deployment
sections.summary: By formalizing a Hierarchical MDP on topological graphs, this work resolves sample efficiency bottlenecks in closed-loop RL for VLN-CE to achieve SOTA. Future directions include removing reliance on waypoint predictors and upgrading heuristic low-level controllers for real-world robotics.
sections.details:
This work reformulates continuous Vision-Language Navigation as a Hierarchical MDP and abstracts the physical environment into a topological graph, practicalizing closed-loop reinforcement learning previously held back by intractable decision horizons. Using graph-based PPO with an Action-Aware Value Head suited for dynamic action spaces, the agent autonomously overcomes the distribution shift and path deviation dilemmas inherent to imitation learning.

The authors also candidly discuss limitations. The current framework relies on local candidate proposals generated by a waypoint predictor, meaning theoretical global reachability across any point in space is not guaranteed. Furthermore, because the low-level controller relies on simple heuristics, transferring this approach to real robots (Sim-to-Real) will require integration with more robust local navigation algorithms capable of handling physical obstacles.

takeaways: In long-horizon continuous navigation, elevating the RL action space from low-level motor controls to high-level topological graph frontiers compresses decision steps, making closed-loop RL under sparse rewards practical.

In graph environments where action candidates shift dynamically, the Critic must be designed as 'Action-Aware' by receiving candidate frontiers; otherwise, it cannot properly estimate state values for situations like dead ends.

Performance gains from reinforcement learning fine-tuning (RFT) are orthogonal to pre-training dataset scaling, directly resolving the trajectory deviation failures inherent to imitation learning (DAgger).
limitations: Macro action candidates are constrained by the output distribution of an external waypoint predictor, meaning theoretical reachability to arbitrary points across the entire environment is not guaranteed.
The low-level controller relies on simple turn-and-move heuristics, leaving a Sim-to-Real gap when handling dynamic obstacle avoidance on physical robot platforms.
